newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWB Report-Australia looks to Pakistan tender.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWB Report-Australia looks to Pakistan tender.

text.p: Pakistan was expected to tender for 312,000 tonnes of Australian or U.S. white wheat, while Egypt was anticipated to buy as much as 500,000 tonnes of wheat, the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said in its weekly report.
Last week the AWB sold 50,000 tonnes to Sri Lanka, with Argentina also selling 50,000 tonnes to this market, it said.
Other AWB sales reported included 60,000 tonnes of Australian Hard wheat to Sudan and 22,000 tonnes to Kenya, it said.
In the barley market, Australia was seen as selling about 200,000 tonnes of barley to Saudi Arabia in its 1.2 million tonne tender. Canada was reported to have sold the same tonnage, AWB said.
The bulk of the Saudi tender went to Europe, the AWB said.
Iran also bought European Union (EU) barley at A$169.60 a tonne fob for February delivery, it said.
The EU barley subsidy last week was A$44.00 a tonne while its the wheat subsidy about A$2.00 a tonne, AWB said.
Concerns about the future of the U.S. winter wheat crop were allayed last week when snow fell over much of the Hard Red Winter wheat area, it said.
The only surprise now possible from USDA figures due on Monday would be an addition to the area sown to Soft Red Winter wheat or an increase in the amount of wheat used as feed.
The focus would also be on domestic corn feeding figures, it said.
On the Australian domestic scene, attention was swinging to the feed grain market, AWB said.
In Victoria, the dairy industry was showing significant interest in pricing grain forward and at present led the market.
In the northern states, attention had swung to barley as producers cleared out storage to make room for the sorghum crop.
In Queensland, an early sorghum harvest could begin at the end of January, with the bulk of the better than 500,000 tonne crop to be available in March or April, it said.
The domestic market has this priced at A$130.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane but growers are not attracted by that price, it said.
Export parity, set by aggressive Argentine sales, was about A$115.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane and could be expected to kick in during the season, it said.
Feed wheat was presently priced at A$150.00 a tonne, delivered Brisbane. At these prices, sorghum would become the grain of preference in all rations, it said.

The lot feeding industry showed little sign of revival. Producers were finding it difficult to price finished cattle forward and, left with all of the risk, would probably elect to buy grain as needed rather than price it forward, it said.
"They are certainly showing little interest at this stage of the season," it said.
The AWB has maintained its estimate of the national wheat crop at 21.5 million tonnes.
